items.prompt: An application in multiple Availability Zones needs a shared POSIX filesystem. What placement should the architect expect for Amazon EFS?
constraints: Clients run in more than one Availability Zone.
The filesystem must be shared.
Network latency and availability matter.

options.text: Use an EFS Regional filesystem with mount targets in the required Availability Zones and connect clients through the appropriate VPC paths.
Attach one EBS volume simultaneously to every client without cluster coordination.
Create one EFS mount target in another Region and route all clients there.
Copy the filesystem to each client because EFS cannot be shared.

feedback.Reason: Regional EFS is designed for shared file access across Availability Zones through mount targets.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS mount targets provide network access to a file system from a VPC and are placed per Availability Zone for local client paths.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner creates the required mount targets, security-group rules, and client mounts in each workload zone.
Details.errorCorrection: EBS is not a general shared POSIX filesystem, cross-Region access adds the wrong dependency, and EFS is explicitly shareable.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Additional mount targets and cross-AZ traffic have cost and network implications.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EBS multi-attach does not replace a coordinated shared filesystem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A Regional EFS design uses local VPC access, not a remote-Region mount target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EFS supports concurrent network file access.

items.prompt: A workload can tolerate a single Availability Zone and prioritizes the lowest EFS regional footprint cost. Which option should be evaluated?
constraints: The workload has a documented AZ-loss tolerance.
A backup or replication plan exists.
The filesystem access pattern is compatible.

options.text: Evaluate EFS One Zone with an explicit backup or replication design and confirm that its single-AZ durability and availability boundary meets the requirement.
Use One Zone silently for a workload that requires AZ-level resilience.
Use EBS Multi-Attach as a cross-AZ file service.
Use an S3 bucket because every POSIX application can use object semantics unchanged.

feedback.Reason: EFS One Zone can reduce cost but changes the failure-domain and protection decision.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: One Zone storage keeps the file system data in one Availability Zone, unlike Regional EFS.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect records the failure assumption, enables appropriate backup or replication, and verifies application recovery before selecting it.
Details.errorCorrection: Using One Zone against an AZ-resilience requirement is unsafe, EBS is block storage, and S3 is not transparent POSIX storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower cost comes with a narrower availability and durability boundary and recovery dependency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The failure-domain choice must be explicit and aligned with the requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EBS does not provide a general cross-AZ shared file namespace.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object APIs and POSIX file semantics are different.

items.prompt: A latency-sensitive web tier uses EFS for shared configuration and requires the lowest file-operation latency. Which performance mode is the usual starting point?
constraints: The workload is latency-sensitive.
The clients use NFS.
The filesystem does not require Max I/O scale characteristics.

options.text: Start with EFS General Purpose performance mode, then benchmark the actual file-operation pattern and client path.
Choose Max I/O solely because its name implies lower latency.
Use archive storage for the hot configuration files.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule to control NFS operation latency.

feedback.Reason: General Purpose is the EFS mode intended for lower latency for most workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS performance modes trade file-operation latency and scale characteristics; General Purpose is the common latency-oriented choice.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures metadata and data operations from clients near their mount targets and validates the application SLO.
Details.errorCorrection: Max I/O is not selected merely by name, archive is not a hot tier, and S3 lifecycle rules do not control NFS latency.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The best mode depends on client count, operation mix, and current service capabilities, so a representative benchmark remains necessary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Max I/O has different scale and latency trade-offs and is not automatically lower latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Archive or infrequent tiers are inappropriate for hot configuration access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object lifecycle controls storage placement, not file-operation latency.

items.prompt: A shared analytics filesystem will have thousands of clients and highly parallel access. Which EFS decision should be evaluated?
constraints: Client count is very high.
The workload can tolerate a different latency profile.
Parallel access is more important than single-operation latency.

options.text: Evaluate EFS Max I/O performance mode against client scale, operation latency, throughput, and application behavior using a representative load test.
Choose General Purpose without checking the documented client and throughput scale.
Use one EBS volume for every client with no coordination.
Move the clients to S3 without changing their filesystem API.

feedback.Reason: Max I/O is a candidate for highly parallel workloads when its latency trade-off is acceptable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS performance modes have different scale and latency characteristics, so client count and operation mix drive the choice.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests concurrent clients, metadata operations, throughput, and tail latency before adopting the mode.
Details.errorCorrection: Ignoring scale can create a performance ceiling, EBS is not a shared file namespace, and S3 requires an API or application change.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Greater parallel scale can come with higher per-operation latency and should be justified by workload measurements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: General Purpose may not fit the largest parallel client profile without testing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EBS attachment and filesystem coordination do not provide this shared service model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 object access is not transparent to a POSIX application.

items.prompt: A file workload has bursty throughput and low average storage activity. Which EFS throughput model should be considered first?
constraints: Demand varies over time.
Average throughput is materially below peaks.
The workload can tolerate burst behavior.

options.text: Evaluate EFS Bursting Throughput against the file-system size, baseline, peak demand, and burst-credit behavior.
Provision maximum throughput permanently without measuring the workload.
Choose EBS because all bursty file workloads require block storage.
Use storage class transitions to create instantaneous network throughput.

feedback.Reason: Bursting Throughput can fit variable demand when the baseline and credits meet the workload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS bursting provides baseline throughput related to stored data and permits higher bursts within the service model.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models peak duration, monitors burst credits and throughput, and confirms that the application does not depend on indefinite peak throughput.
Details.errorCorrection: Permanent provisioning may overpay, EBS changes semantics, and storage class movement does not create network capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long or repeated peaks can exhaust the performance margin and require a different throughput model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A permanently provisioned maximum may be unnecessary for bursty demand.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Shared file semantics can be met by EFS without switching to block storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage classes affect storage cost and access, not instantaneous network throughput.

items.prompt: A small EFS filesystem has a sustained throughput requirement that exceeds its size-based baseline. What option should the architect compare?
constraints: Throughput is sustained.
File-system size is not expected to grow enough to raise baseline.
The application has a measurable MiB/s target.

options.text: Evaluate Provisioned Throughput at the required sustained level and compare its cost, limits, and monitored usage with other EFS throughput modes.
Artificially store extra data solely to increase the baseline without a cost review.
Rely on burst credits for an indefinite sustained requirement.
Use a larger EBS volume as a transparent replacement for shared EFS.

feedback.Reason: Provisioned Throughput decouples sustained EFS throughput from a small file-system size when the requirement justifies it.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS provisioned throughput supplies a configured throughput level subject to service limits and billing.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner provisions only the measured requirement, monitors utilization, and periodically reviews whether the mode remains economical.
Details.errorCorrection: Artificial data wastes capacity, burst credits are not indefinite, and EBS does not transparently provide EFS shared-file behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned throughput adds cost and can be wasteful when demand is intermittent or the filesystem grows naturally.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Adding data to manipulate baseline creates storage cost and is not a sound capacity decision.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Credits cannot guarantee an indefinite sustained rate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EBS has a different attachment and access model.

items.prompt: A new EFS workload has unpredictable peaks and the team does not want to forecast throughput capacity manually. Which design should be evaluated?
constraints: Peak demand is variable.
Operational simplicity matters.
The current Region and account support the selected feature.

options.text: Evaluate EFS Elastic Throughput, including its pricing, service limits, regional availability, and monitored workload behavior.
Choose a fixed throughput value without measuring peaks or cost.
Increase file-system capacity indefinitely to guarantee network throughput.
Use a tape gateway to absorb interactive file-operation spikes.

feedback.Reason: Elastic Throughput is a candidate when EFS throughput demand is unpredictable and the feature fits the workload and commercial constraints.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Elastic Throughput automatically scales throughput for eligible workloads and charges according to the service model.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner confirms feature support, sets cost controls, and observes throughput and latency under real peak patterns.
Details.errorCorrection: Fixed values can under- or over-provision, capacity is not an unlimited network control, and tape storage is not interactive file access.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Elasticity can simplify planning but has usage cost and service-limit considerations that must be reviewed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A fixed value is not aligned with intentionally unpredictable peaks unless measured and justified.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity growth is not a universal guarantee of required throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Tape-oriented gateways do not provide low-latency shared file operations.

items.prompt: Multiple teams share one EFS filesystem but must be restricted to separate application directories and identities. What EFS feature helps establish the boundary?
constraints: The applications use POSIX file access.
Directory and identity isolation are required.
The filesystem is shared by design.

options.text: Use EFS access points with configured root directories and POSIX user or group identity enforcement, then apply least-privilege network access.
Rely only on the application naming convention for directory isolation.
Create a new EBS volume for each process and mount them all cross-AZ.
Use an S3 bucket policy to enforce NFS directory ownership.

feedback.Reason: EFS access points provide application-specific entry points and POSIX identity and directory controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An access point can enforce a root directory and POSIX user or group for NFS clients.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner maps each service to an access point, limits IAM and network permissions, and validates the resulting filesystem ownership.
Details.errorCorrection: Naming conventions do not enforce isolation, EBS is not the shared file service, and S3 policies do not govern NFS paths.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Access points simplify boundaries but do not replace file permissions, encryption, network controls, or application authorization.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A convention is not an enforcement mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EBS does not provide this shared multi-client filesystem model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 bucket policies govern object requests, not EFS NFS path ownership.

items.prompt: An EC2 client intermittently loses EFS performance because it uses an unsuitable mount path and options. What should the operator verify?
constraints: The client is in the same VPC as the filesystem.
The NFS client package is supported.
Latency and throughput are measurable.

options.text: Verify the recommended EFS mount helper or NFS options, DNS and mount-target resolution, security groups, and the client's network placement.
Increase the EFS storage class because mount options cannot affect access.
Attach the EFS filesystem as a raw block device.
Disable all NFS safeguards to maximize throughput without testing.

feedback.Reason: EFS is a network filesystem and client mount configuration and path selection affect observed behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS clients connect through mount targets using NFS and supported helpers or options.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates the mount command, DNS, security-group rules, network path, and client metrics before tuning the filesystem.
Details.errorCorrection: Storage class does not fix a network mount, EFS is not a raw block device, and disabling safeguards risks correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Mount tuning can change consistency, throughput, and failure behavior and should be tested with the application.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Storage classes affect data placement and cost, not client mount correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EFS exposes a file protocol, not an attachable block device.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unreviewed NFS changes can trade throughput for correctness or resilience.

items.prompt: An EFS design adds clients and throughput but tail latency rises sharply. Which review should come before changing storage service?
constraints: The file system is shared by many clients.
The workload has metadata and data operations.
Client and EFS metrics are available.

options.text: Correlate client count, operation mix, NFS latency, throughput mode, burst or provisioned limits, network path, and hot-directory behavior before changing the service.
Assume adding clients always increases throughput linearly.
Increase file permissions because authorization is the usual cause of tail latency.
Move all clients to one Availability Zone without measuring network cost or failure impact.

feedback.Reason: Shared file performance depends on client concurrency, operation mix, network path, and throughput mode rather than client count alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS exposes network file operations whose queueing and metadata behavior can create a tail-latency bottleneck.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect profiles the workload, tests mount-target placement and throughput settings, and changes the service only after identifying the constraint.
Details.errorCorrection: Scaling clients can increase contention, permissions do not normally explain throughput saturation, and single-AZ concentration harms resilience.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A different filesystem may fit a specialized parallel workload, but migration and semantics must be considered.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shared access can contend and is not linearly scalable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Permissions are a correctness and security concern, not a generic latency fix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Concentration can reduce network distance in one case but creates failure and cost trade-offs.

items.prompt: An EFS filesystem contains hot project files and older files that are rarely read but must remain available. What design is appropriate?
constraints: The application uses a shared file namespace.
Older data can tolerate slower first access.
Access patterns can be measured.

options.text: Use EFS lifecycle management to move eligible files to an infrequent-access class while keeping hot files in the standard class, and test access latency.
Move all data to archive because the namespace is shared.
Increase EFS throughput to make cold storage free.
Delete old files without checking retention or recovery requirements.

feedback.Reason: EFS storage classes can align cost with access frequency without changing the shared filesystem model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS lifecycle management moves files between standard and infrequent-access classes based on age and access policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner defines a policy from measured access and validates the first-read latency and retrieval cost for older files.
Details.errorCorrection: Archive-like treatment can violate access needs, throughput does not eliminate storage cost, and deletion needs retention approval.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Infrequent access reduces storage cost but can add access charges and latency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cold data can remain available without moving every file to the coldest tier.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Throughput capacity and storage pricing are separate decisions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retention and recovery must be preserved for data that remains required.

items.prompt: A Windows application requires SMB shares, Windows ACL behavior, and native file-server semantics. Which AWS service should be evaluated?
constraints: The application requires SMB.
Windows identity and ACLs matter.
The workload needs managed file storage.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, including SMB compatibility, Active Directory integration, performance, and deployment type.
Use EFS because every network filesystem exposes SMB and Windows ACLs identically.
Use S3 and mount it as a native SMB file server without an adapter.
Use an EBS volume attached to multiple Windows servers without cluster-aware coordination.

feedback.Reason: FSx for Windows File Server is the managed service aligned with SMB and Windows file-server semantics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for Windows provides SMB file shares and integrates with Microsoft Active Directory for identity and ACL scenarios.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects Single-AZ or Multi-AZ based on resilience, joins the right directory, and tests share permissions and throughput.
Details.errorCorrection: EFS uses NFS, S3 is object storage, and raw EBS sharing requires a separate coordinated cluster design.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Windows file semantics and managed features come with service, directory, and cost constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: EFS NFS semantics are not an SMB Windows file-server replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 does not expose native SMB without an additional service or adapter.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EBS attachment is block storage and does not provide coordinated SMB file serving.

items.prompt: An FSx for Windows deployment must preserve existing domain users and file ACLs. What integration is central?
constraints: An Active Directory domain already exists.
Users and groups must retain identity semantics.
The file shares are accessed over SMB.

options.text: Integrate the file system with the appropriate AWS Managed Microsoft AD or self-managed Active Directory and validate DNS, network, trust, and permissions.
Create local file-system users with names matching domain users but no directory integration.
Use an IAM policy as a replacement for Windows share and NTFS authorization.
Disable ACLs so all domain users can access every share.

feedback.Reason: FSx Windows identity and ACL behavior depends on directory integration and a functioning network and DNS path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for Windows uses Active Directory for authentication and Windows file permissions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner confirms domain connectivity, service accounts, DNS, organizational-unit requirements, and tests effective permissions.
Details.errorCorrection: Matching local names does not preserve identities, IAM is not NTFS authorization, and disabling ACLs violates least privilege.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Directory dependencies can affect provisioning and availability, so the design needs operational ownership and recovery procedures.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Local accounts are different security principals from domain users.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM controls AWS API access, not Windows share and NTFS permissions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Removing ACL controls creates an authorization failure, not a valid migration.

items.prompt: A Windows file share must remain available through an Availability Zone failure. Which FSx deployment choice should be compared?
constraints: The application needs continuous file access during an AZ event.
SMB semantics are required.
The recovery objective is shorter than a manual restore.

options.text: Evaluate FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ, including its failover behavior, network paths, directory dependencies, and cost.
Choose Single-AZ and rely on a nightly copy for a near-zero interruption objective.
Use EFS One Zone because Windows SMB clients have no failure-domain needs.
Use a local instance store share because it is automatically replicated.

feedback.Reason: Multi-AZ FSx is a candidate when the managed Windows file service must tolerate an AZ failure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx deployment types provide different availability and failover boundaries; Multi-AZ is designed for high availability across AZs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests SMB reconnect behavior, DNS, application retry, and directory availability as part of the failover plan.
Details.errorCorrection: A nightly copy cannot meet near-zero interruption, EFS does not provide Windows SMB semantics, and instance store is ephemeral.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multi-AZ improves resilience but costs more and does not remove application and directory dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A copy-based recovery has an interruption and data-loss window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EFS uses NFS and is not a Windows SMB service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance store is not automatically replicated or durable.

items.prompt: A compute cluster processes large files in parallel and requires a high-throughput shared POSIX filesystem. Which service is a strong candidate?
constraints: The workload is parallel.
Large sequential and parallel I/O dominates.
The data can be staged or regenerated.

options.text: Evaluate FSx for Lustre using the required deployment, throughput per TiB, client network path, and data staging or export design.
Use FSx for Windows because every parallel Linux workload requires SMB.
Use a single gp3 volume because shared parallel compute cannot use a file system.
Use S3 directly as a POSIX shared block device without an integration layer.

feedback.Reason: FSx for Lustre targets high-performance parallel file workloads and integrates with data repositories such as S3.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Lustre provides a parallel file system with configurable throughput and deployment options for compute-intensive workloads.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect sizes clients and filesystem throughput together, stages input, exports results, and plans failure and rebuild behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: FSx Windows targets SMB, one EBS volume cannot provide this shared parallel service, and S3 is object storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lustre performance depends on client networking and costs; it is not automatically the best general-purpose file system.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Windows SMB semantics are a different workload fit from Lustre POSIX parallel I/O.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A single block volume does not provide shared parallel file access to the cluster.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 needs an integration or application interface and is not a POSIX block device.

items.prompt: A batch analytics job reads inputs from S3 through a high-performance filesystem and exports results back to S3. What should be designed explicitly?
constraints: S3 is the durable data repository.
The compute job needs filesystem semantics during execution.
Input and output synchronization matter.

options.text: Use an FSx for Lustre deployment integrated with S3 where appropriate, and define import, export, permissions, consistency, and job lifecycle behavior.
Assume every S3 object is instantly a local Lustre file without import or export semantics.
Use EFS and assume it automatically presents an S3 bucket as a local mount.
Store the only copy on the temporary filesystem and delete the S3 data after import.

feedback.Reason: The S3-linked Lustre pattern has explicit data movement and consistency boundaries.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for Lustre can link a file system to S3, but import and export operations and permissions must be designed.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner defines when inputs are imported, when results are exported, how failed jobs retry, and which repository is authoritative.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 objects are not automatically local files at all times, EFS has no transparent S3 mount, and deleting the durable source is unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The integration simplifies staging but introduces synchronization, permissions, and lifecycle considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 integration has explicit import and export semantics and does not remove synchronization design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: EFS is a file service and does not transparently mount an S3 bucket.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Temporary compute storage is not a durable system of record.

items.prompt: A Linux application needs a managed NFS file system with low-latency metadata operations and ZFS features. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: NFS semantics are required.
The application benefits from ZFS capabilities.
The workload is not an SMB workload.

options.text: Evaluate FSx for OpenZFS, including NFS version, deployment type, throughput, IOPS, snapshot behavior, and client compatibility.
Choose FSx for Windows because all managed file systems use NFS identically.
Choose S3 because object storage has native POSIX snapshots.
Use an EBS boot volume as a multi-client NFS service without an NFS server.

feedback.Reason: FSx for OpenZFS is the managed service candidate for NFS workloads that need OpenZFS characteristics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for OpenZFS provides managed OpenZFS file systems and NFS access with configurable performance and deployment options.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect checks the required NFS version, snapshot and clone behavior, client path, and recovery needs.
Details.errorCorrection: FSx Windows is SMB-oriented, S3 is object storage, and an EBS volume is not an NFS service by itself.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ZFS features and performance tiers add service-specific limits and cost that must fit the workload.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Windows file service is centered on SMB and Active Directory rather than this NFS fit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 does not provide native POSIX snapshots.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Block storage needs a separate server and coordination layer to serve NFS.

items.prompt: An enterprise file service must support NFS, SMB, and multiprotocol data management with ONTAP-style features. Which service is the relevant candidate?
constraints: Multiple file protocols are required.
The organization has ONTAP operational knowledge.
Identity and data management requirements are known.

options.text: Evaluate FSx for NetApp ONTAP, including supported protocols, storage virtual machines, deployment type, throughput, and identity integration.
Use EFS and assume SMB and NFS permissions are interchangeable.
Use FSx for Windows and mount it with native NFS without checking supported protocols.
Use an S3 bucket as a multiprotocol file server without an access layer.

feedback.Reason: FSx for NetApp ONTAP is designed for managed ONTAP file-service patterns and multiple protocol choices.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx for ONTAP provides storage virtual machines and file access options that can include NFS and SMB, subject to service configuration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect maps protocol, identity, snapshot, replication, performance, and cutover requirements to the ONTAP design.
Details.errorCorrection: EFS and Windows FSx have different protocol and permission models, and S3 is not a multiprotocol file server.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ONTAP flexibility increases configuration and operational responsibility and should be justified by the file-service requirements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: NFS and SMB permission models are not interchangeable by assumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Protocol support and configuration must be verified rather than inferred from a Windows label.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 needs an explicit application or gateway interface for file access.

items.prompt: A distributed compute site repeatedly reads the same on-premises file data and needs a cloud cache while the source remains authoritative. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: The source data remains on premises.
Cloud workloads need repeated low-latency reads.
The cache can be repopulated.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon File Cache as a managed cache for file data, with connectivity, namespace, freshness, and source-of-truth behavior documented.
Use EBS snapshots as a live shared cache for on-premises NFS clients.
Use S3 replication and assume it preserves live file-lock semantics.
Use a tape gateway because cache misses are archival operations.

feedback.Reason: File Cache is designed to provide a cloud cache for file data from supported on-premises or cloud sources.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Amazon File Cache presents a high-performance cache namespace while the linked data repository remains authoritative.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates data freshness, write behavior, network connectivity, cache population, and recovery when the cache is unavailable.
Details.errorCorrection: Snapshots are point-in-time copies, S3 replication does not preserve file locks, and tape is not an interactive cache.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A cache introduces freshness and repopulation dependencies and should not be treated as the only durable copy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Snapshots do not provide a live multi-client cache service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object replication does not automatically preserve filesystem locking and namespace semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Tape access is not a low-latency cache path.

items.prompt: A file system has enough capacity but the workload still misses its throughput target. What sizing distinction matters?
constraints: Capacity is not full.
Throughput is measured at the client.
The chosen service has capacity-linked and provisioned performance dimensions.

options.text: Separate capacity sizing from throughput and IOPS sizing, then select the file-service performance model and client network path that meet the measured target.
Add arbitrary files until the application reaches its throughput target.
Reduce filesystem capacity because less data always means more throughput.
Ignore client network bandwidth because managed storage has unlimited client throughput.

feedback.Reason: File-service capacity, throughput, IOPS, and client network limits are distinct sizing dimensions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Different EFS and FSx modes expose different relationships between stored capacity, configured performance, and client path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect models data growth and measured I/O independently and validates the complete client-to-service route.
Details.errorCorrection: Artificial data is not a valid performance control, reducing capacity can hurt retention, and client bandwidth remains finite.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned performance can meet a small filesystem's target but adds cost and must be monitored.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Artificial capacity is wasteful and does not guarantee the required client throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity reduction does not universally improve file-service performance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The client network path can be the bottleneck even with managed storage.

items.prompt: A shared filesystem contains regulated data and must recover from accidental deletion. Which architecture element is required regardless of the selected file service?
constraints: Recovery from logical deletion is required.
File permissions and snapshots are distinct controls.
The recovery objective is documented.

options.text: Define independent backups or snapshots, retention, restore validation, and application-consistent recovery procedures in addition to the live filesystem choice.
Treat replication or Multi-AZ placement as protection from every user deletion.
Rely on file permissions as a backup mechanism.
Use a performance mode with more throughput because it prevents deletion.

feedback.Reason: Availability and replication do not automatically provide point-in-time recovery from logical deletion.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backups, snapshots, retention, and restore procedures address recovery needs that live access controls and availability do not.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner schedules protected copies, tests restores and permissions, and records the RTO and RPO for the filesystem.
Details.errorCorrection: Replication can copy deletion, permissions do not recover data, and throughput settings do not affect deletion protection.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backup frequency and retention add cost and operational work but are necessary for the stated recovery outcome.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A replicated live namespace can replicate an accidental delete.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Permissions can reduce unauthorized access but are not a recoverable copy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Performance configuration does not change data-protection semantics.

items.prompt: A design review compares EFS, FSx for Windows, FSx for Lustre, FSx for OpenZFS, and FSx for ONTAP. What is the correct selection method?
constraints: The application semantics are known.
Performance and availability targets are explicit.
Migration and operations matter.

options.text: Select from protocol and semantics, access pattern, performance model, failure domain, identity integration, data lifecycle, operational fit, and measured workload requirements.
Choose the service with the largest capacity number regardless of protocol and latency.
Choose EFS for every file workload because all file systems have identical behavior.
Choose the cheapest hourly option without modeling data transfer, backup, and throughput costs.

feedback.Reason: Managed file services solve different protocol, workload, and performance problems and require a multidimensional comparison.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS and FSx services differ in protocol, namespace, performance, deployment, identity, and integration characteristics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect maps the existing application contract and measured signals to one canonical service, then tests migration and recovery.
